claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes high-entropy nanoalloys under high-temperature conditions.
Thermally activated atomic diffusion, especially surface diffusion, destabilizes high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sufficiently activated diffusion can overcome entropy-driven stabilization and cause elemental segregation and phase separation.
Intrinsic lattice distortions slow atomic diffusion.
Diffusion slowed by lattice distortions allows the nanoalloy to retain a homogeneous, single-phase structure.
Enhanced diffusion can drive local chemical-potential gradients and trigger segregation and new-phase formation.
High configurational entropy and localized lattice distortions increase the energetic barrier to atomic rearrangement.
Whether a homogeneous phase is preserved or segregation begins depends on the balance between diffusion and entropy- or distortion-based resistance to rearrangement.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, a high-entropy nanoalloy with intrinsic diffusion-limiting features will remain more homogeneous and single-phase than the proposed baseline.
The proposed baseline is expected to exhibit more elemental segregation and phase decomposition.
The prediction is limited to temperatures that activate diffusion but do not cause melting or uncontrolled grain growth.
The nanoscale surface-to-volume ratio moderates diffusion effects.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in highly reactive atmospheres or when other high-temperature processes dominate.
The temperature threshold and diffusion kinetics relative to the entropy effect may vary with alloy composition and particle size.
The proposed test subjects a high-entropy nanoalloy and a comparison sample to identical annealing conditions in an inert atmosphere.
Similar segregation, phase decomposition, or grain growth in both samples is specified as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome invokes comparison under identical high-temperature conditions, but the baseline is partly defined as the as-synthesized alloy before high-temperature treatment. A pre-treatment sample is not exposed to identical annealing conditions.

The prediction expects the high-entropy sample with diffusion-limiting features to outperform its comparator, whereas the experimental design permits a 'diffusion-inhibited variant' as the comparator. Such a comparator could have the same proposed stabilizing property or stronger diffusion inhibition, so the expected direction is not consistently defined.
